events.fact: The Stamp Act took effect in the American colonies, and the colonists so resolutely refused to use the taxed stamps that daily business nearly halted, forcing Parliament to repeal it within months.
President John Adams became the first to occupy the President's House in Washington, writing the prayer, 'May none but honest and wise men ever rule under this roof.'

block: On November 1, 1765, the Stamp Act took force across the American colonies, and a free-spirited people refused so steadfastly to buy the taxed stamps that commerce ground to a halt and Parliament was driven to repeal the hated law within the year. On the same day in 1800, President John Adams became the first to sleep in the unfinished President's House, where he penned the prayer that none but honest and wise men might ever rule beneath its roof. A Steadfast citizen holds his ground as those colonists did against unjust burden, and labors that his houses of government be filled, as Adams asked of God, with honest and wise men.

events.fact: General George Washington issued his Farewell Orders to the Armies of the United States at Rocky Hill, near Princeton, calling his soldiers 'one patriotic band of Brothers' after eight years of war.
North Dakota and South Dakota were admitted as the 39th and 40th states; President Benjamin Harrison shuffled the papers so none could say which was signed first.

block: On November 2, 1783, after eight long years in the field, General George Washington gave his Farewell Orders to the Armies of the United States at Rocky Hill near Princeton, hailing the men who had endured almost every hardship as 'one patriotic band of Brothers.' On the same day in 1889, President Benjamin Harrison admitted North Dakota and South Dakota as the thirty-ninth and fortieth states, shuffling the signing papers so that neither sister could claim to have entered the Union first. An Enduring citizen learns from Washington's veterans, who bore privation and discouragement to the very end, that the work God sets before a man is finished not by the eager but by those who hold fast through the long years.

events.fact: The Continental Army was officially disbanded at New Windsor, New York, the soldiers laying down their arms and returning to civilian life under the new republic.
The Chicago Daily Tribune ran its mistaken 'Dewey Defeats Truman' headline; the next day Harry Truman held the paper aloft in triumph after his upset victory.

block: On November 3, 1783, Congress formally disbanded the Continental Army at New Windsor, New York, and the men who had won a nation's freedom quietly laid down their muskets and went home to their farms and shops, submitting the sword to the civil order they had fought to establish. On the same day in 1948, the Chicago Daily Tribune rushed to press with the false headline 'Dewey Defeats Truman,' only for the people's actual votes to overturn every confident prediction. A Steadfast citizen takes both lessons to heart, honoring the soldier who holds his post and then yields it lawfully, and trusting that no premature verdict of men can stand against what is true and rightly settled in its appointed hour.

events.fact: Abraham Lincoln married Mary Todd at her sister's home in Springfield, Illinois, after a long and troubled courtship the two had finally resolved.
Richard Jordan Gatling of Indianapolis received U.S. Patent No. 36,836 for his rapid-fire 'Revolving Battery-Gun,' which he hoped would reduce the size of armies and the deaths of war.

block: On November 4, 1842, the struggling lawyer Abraham Lincoln married Mary Todd in her sister's parlor in Springfield, Illinois, binding himself in covenant after a courtship broken off and at last mended through perseverance. On the same day in 1862, the inventor Richard Gatling of Indianapolis received his patent for the revolving battery-gun, the fruit of stubborn labor at his workbench. A Steadfast citizen keeps the vows he makes and the work he begins, refusing to abandon either the wife of his youth or the calling of his hands until, by God's grace, both are brought to good account.

events.fact: John Hanson of Maryland was elected President of the United States in Congress Assembled, the presiding officer of the Continental Congress under the newly ratified Articles of Confederation.
The Gunpowder Plot to blow up the English Parliament was foiled, an event long marked in the American colonies as a deliverance of providence.

block: On November 5, 1781, the Continental Congress chose John Hanson of Maryland to preside as President of the United States in Congress Assembled, a steady moderator entrusted to guide a quarrelsome young union under its first written compact. On the same day in 1605, the Gunpowder Plot to destroy the English Parliament was uncovered before it could be sprung, a deliverance the early colonists long remembered as the hand of God turning back a hidden evil. A Steadfast citizen keeps his post as Hanson kept the chair of a fractious Congress, and remembers that the same Providence which exposed a plot in 1605 still guards the works of men who labor in fidelity before Him.

events.fact: Abraham Lincoln was elected the 16th president of the United States, the first Republican to win the office, on the highest voter turnout the nation had yet seen.
Jefferson Davis was elected to a full six-year term as president of the Confederate States, formalizing the secession that Lincoln's election had set in motion.

block: On November 6, 1860, the people elected Abraham Lincoln the sixteenth president of the United States in a contest that drew more than four of every five eligible men to the polls, only for seven states to begin tearing the Union apart before he could be sworn in. One year later, on November 6, 1861, the Southern states elected Jefferson Davis to a full term as president of their Confederacy, hardening the division into open and bloody war. An Obedient citizen submits himself to the lawful order of elections and offices even when his countrymen are bitterly divided, trusting the God who raises up rulers and casts them down to govern the storms that men cannot.

events.fact: Abraham Lincoln was re-elected president in the midst of the Civil War, the Union holding a free national election while armies were still in the field.
Montana was admitted as the 41st state of the Union by proclamation of President Benjamin Harrison.

block: On November 8, 1864, the Union held a free presidential election in the very midst of civil war and returned Abraham Lincoln to office, proving that a republic could keep faith with its own laws while its soldiers were still under fire. On the same day in 1889, President Benjamin Harrison proclaimed Montana the forty-first state, drawing the high northern frontier under the settled government of the Union. A Steadfast citizen treasures both: a people who would not suspend their liberties even in war, and a nation that steadily grew without abandoning the order it was built upon, holding firm to the constitutional path God's providence had marked out.

events.fact: After sixty-six days at sea, the passengers of the Mayflower sighted the shore of Cape Cod at sunrise, their first glimpse of the New World.
NASA launched Apollo 4, the first flight of the 363-foot Saturn V rocket, a complete success that proved the machine that would carry men to the moon.

block: On November 9, 1620, after sixty-six storm-tossed days upon the Atlantic, the weary passengers of the Mayflower at last sighted the low shore of Cape Cod at dawn, their first sight of the land where they would plant a godly commonwealth. On the same day in 1967, NASA sent the towering Saturn V skyward for the first time as Apollo 4, a flawless test of the rocket that would soon bear men to the moon. A Steadfast citizen reads in both voyages the same virtue, for whether crossing an ocean toward an unknown coast or thundering toward the heavens, it is the man who endures the long passage who reaches the shore God has set before him.

events.fact: The Second Continental Congress resolved to raise two battalions of Marines, founding the United States Marine Corps, with Samuel Nicholas commissioned as its first officer at Philadelphia.
The first coast-to-coast direct-dial telephone call was placed, connecting Englewood, New Jersey to Alameda, California automatically in eighteen seconds without an operator.

block: On November 10, 1775, the Second Continental Congress resolved that two battalions of Marines be raised, founding the Corps whose riflemen would fight on sea and shore, and commissioned Samuel Nicholas as its first officer in Philadelphia. On the same day in 1951, the first direct-dial telephone call spanned the continent, joining a mayor in New Jersey to a mayor in California in eighteen seconds with no operator between them. An Obedient citizen honors the Marine who answers the lawful call to arms and stands his post under orders, and the patient labor of honest men whose discipline knit a whole nation together so that one voice could reach another across three thousand miles.

events.fact: The Armistice ending the First World War took effect at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month, the day later honored as Veterans Day.
The Pilgrims aboard the Mayflower signed the Mayflower Compact in Provincetown Harbor, covenanting together to form a civil body politic for the glory of God and the general good.

block: On November 11, 1918, the guns of the Great War fell silent at the eleventh hour of the eleventh day of the eleventh month, a day America keeps still to honor every veteran who answered his country's call. On the same day in 1620, the men of the Mayflower set their hands to the Compact in the harbor at Provincetown, covenanting before God and one another to frame just laws for the common good of their little colony. A Loyal citizen stands by both bonds, keeping faith with the soldiers who laid down their lives for their brothers and with the solemn covenant of self-government our forefathers swore in the name of God.

events.fact: The astronomer Andrew Ellicott, observing the Leonids from a ship off the Florida Keys, recorded the first known account of a meteor shower in North America.
Ellis Island closed its doors after sixty-two years, having received more than twelve million immigrants seeking a new home in America.

block: On November 12, 1799, the American surveyor and astronomer Andrew Ellicott, watching the Leonids blaze over the sea off the Florida Keys, set down the first honest record of a meteor shower seen in North America, faithful to note exactly what his eyes beheld. On the same day in 1954, Ellis Island closed at last, its gates having welcomed more than twelve million souls who came to build new lives under American liberty. An Upright citizen keeps a true and exact account as Ellicott did of the heavens, and deals honestly with the stranger seeking an honest start, for the God who set the stars in their courses also numbers every man who passes through the gate.

events.fact: The Vietnam Veterans Memorial was dedicated in Washington, its black granite wall inscribed with the names of the 57,939 Americans then known to have died in the conflict.
The Holland Tunnel opened beneath the Hudson River, the first underwater vehicular crossing between Manhattan and New Jersey, carrying more than fifty-two thousand cars on its first day.

block: On November 13, 1982, the Vietnam Veterans Memorial was dedicated in Washington, its long wall of black granite bearing the names of the more than fifty-seven thousand Americans then counted among the war's fallen, that the nation might keep faith with every one. On the same day in 1927, the Holland Tunnel opened beneath the Hudson River as the first underwater road crossing in the country, the work of engineers whose careful labor bore the weight of fifty-two thousand vehicles its very first day. A Trustworthy citizen honors both, keeping faith with the dead whose names are graven in stone and building, as those engineers built, work so sound and honest that men may stake their lives upon it.

events.fact: Herman Melville's novel 'Moby-Dick' was published in America, a sprawling sea-tale of obsession and Providence that became a cornerstone of American letters.
Apollo 12 lifted off from Kennedy Space Center; though struck by lightning twice in its first minute, it pressed on to make the second manned landing on the moon.

block: On November 14, 1851, Herman Melville gave America 'Moby-Dick,' a vast and brooding account of one man's relentless pursuit across the sea, fruit of years of solitary labor at his desk. On the same day in 1969, Apollo 12 thundered off the pad at Cape Kennedy and, though lightning struck the rocket twice within the first minute of flight, the crew held their nerve and carried the mission on to a second landing upon the moon. A Steadfast citizen presses on as Melville did through long years of writing and as Conrad and Bean did through the lightning, refusing to be turned aside from the course God has given him to finish.

events.fact: The Continental Congress, meeting at York, Pennsylvania, adopted the Articles of Confederation, the first constitution of the United States.
Zebulon Pike sighted the great Colorado mountain that would bear his name, recording it first as a small blue cloud on the western horizon.

block: On November 15, 1777, the Continental Congress, driven from Philadelphia to the little town of York, Pennsylvania, by advancing British troops, adopted the Articles of Confederation as the first written charter binding the states into one government. On the same day in 1806, the explorer Zebulon Pike spied a faint blue cloud on the far horizon that proved to be the towering peak now bearing his name, a summit he submitted himself to seek though he never reached its top. An Obedient citizen takes his ordered place under lawful government as the framers at York intended, and presses toward the heights set before him, bowing to the discipline of the long road as Pike did beneath his mountain.

events.fact: The United States Congress convened for the first time in the new Capitol at Washington, D.C., establishing the permanent seat of the national government.
President Richard Nixon declared 'I am not a crook' before newspaper editors in Orlando, a denial that became a turning point in the Watergate scandal that ended his presidency.

block: On November 17, 1800, the Congress of the United States gathered for the first time in the new Capitol at Washington, settling the national government at last upon its permanent and lawful seat. On the same day in 1973, President Richard Nixon stood before the nation's editors in Orlando and insisted, 'I am not a crook,' a hollow denial that hastened the unraveling of his own presidency. A Steadfast citizen reveres the enduring house of government raised in 1800 and learns from 1973 that no office, however high, can long stand upon falsehood, for only what is built and held in truth abides under the eye of God.

events.fact: Captain Nathaniel Palmer of Stonington, Connecticut, only twenty-two and commanding the sloop Hero, became the first American to sight the mainland of Antarctica; Palmer Land bears his name.
American and Canadian railroads adopted Standard Time, dividing the continent into time zones so that a single ordered reckoning of hours could govern travel and commerce.

block: On November 18, 1820, the young Connecticut sea-captain Nathaniel Palmer, sailing the little sloop Hero at the age of twenty-two, became the first American to lay eyes on the mainland of Antarctica, a coast and a land that still bear his name. On the same day in 1883, the railroads of America and Canada set their watches together and adopted Standard Time, bringing the whole continent under one honest and common reckoning of the hours. A Trustworthy citizen ventures faithfully into the hard and unknown places as Palmer did, and keeps true time with his neighbor as the railroads taught a nation to do, for a man whose word and whose clock can be relied upon is a gift from God to all around him.

events.fact: President Abraham Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery, resolving in fewer than three hundred words that the dead 'shall not have died in vain.'
James A. Garfield, twentieth president of the United States and a lay preacher of the Disciples of Christ, was born in a log cabin in Orange Township, Ohio.

block: On November 19, 1863, President Abraham Lincoln rose at the dedication of the Soldiers' National Cemetery at Gettysburg and, in fewer than three hundred words, resolved that the honored dead should not have died in vain and that government of the people should not perish from the earth. On the same day in 1831, James A. Garfield, who would become the twentieth president and who preached the gospel as a lay minister before he ever held office, was born in a log cabin in Orange Township, Ohio. A Steadfast citizen draws strength from both, from Lincoln's vow to finish the work the fallen began and from Garfield's rise from a cabin floor, resolving to stand firm in his labor and his faith and to leave nothing God has set before him undone.

events.fact: New Jersey became the first state to ratify the Bill of Rights, approving eleven of the twelve amendments then proposed to the Constitution.
The Nuremberg trials of the principal Nazi war criminals opened before an international tribunal, holding even the mighty to account under the rule of law.

block: On November 20, 1789, New Jersey led all her sister states by becoming the first to ratify the Bill of Rights, fixing in the supreme law the liberties of conscience, speech, and worship that guard a free people. On the same day in 1945, the surviving leaders of Nazi Germany were brought before the international tribunal at Nuremberg, where even the once-mighty were made to answer for monstrous crimes under the rule of law. A Steadfast citizen holds fast to both pillars, cherishing the secured liberties that no government may strip away and upholding the steady principle that no man, however powerful, stands above the justice ordained by God.

events.fact: The pirate Blackbeard, Edward Teach, was killed in battle at Ocracoke Inlet off North Carolina by a Royal Navy force under Lieutenant Robert Maynard, sent by Virginia's Governor Spotswood.
President John F. Kennedy was assassinated in Dallas, Texas, a national grief that fell upon the country in a single hour.

block: On November 22, 1718, the dreaded pirate Blackbeard was run to ground and killed at Ocracoke Inlet off the Carolina coast by a Royal Navy party under Lieutenant Robert Maynard, dispatched by Virginia's Governor Spotswood to end his plunder of honest shipping. On the same day in 1963, President John F. Kennedy was struck down by an assassin's bullet in Dallas, and a sudden grief swept over the whole nation. A Steadfast citizen takes both to heart, supporting the lawful sword that puts down the lawless, and standing firm when calamity falls without warning, anchored in the God whose purposes are not overturned by the violence of men.

events.fact: Union forces under General Joseph Hooker stormed Lookout Mountain near Chattanooga in the fog-shrouded 'Battle Above the Clouds,' breaking the Confederate left and helping lift the siege.
The crew of Apollo 12 returned safely to Earth after the second manned landing on the moon, completing a flight of ten days and four hours.

block: On November 24, 1863, Union troops under General Joseph Hooker climbed and seized Lookout Mountain above Chattanooga in a mist so thick the fight was called the 'Battle Above the Clouds,' breaking the enemy line and opening the way to relieve the besieged army below. On the same day in 1969, the astronauts of Apollo 12 splashed down safely after their voyage to the moon, the duty entrusted to them faithfully discharged. A Responsible citizen takes up the task laid on him as Hooker's men took the mountain and as those astronauts brought their ship home, answering for the charge given him and seeing it through to the end before God and his fellows.

events.fact: British troops evacuated New York City on Evacuation Day, and General George Washington led the Continental Army in triumph down through Manhattan to the Battery.
General John Forbes, with Colonel George Washington in his column, took possession of the ruined Fort Duquesne, securing the forks of the Ohio where Pittsburgh would rise.

block: On November 25, 1783, the last British troops at last departed New York Harbor on Evacuation Day, and General George Washington rode in triumph down through Manhattan to the Battery, the long war for independence finally won. On the same day in 1758, after years of frontier struggle, General John Forbes, with the young Colonel Washington among his officers, marched into the smoldering ruins of Fort Duquesne and claimed the forks of the Ohio where the city of Pittsburgh would one day stand. A Steadfast citizen sees in both days the reward of perseverance, for the same Washington who at last freed New York had years before pressed through the wilderness to a hard-won fort, proof that the God of armies honors the man who endures to the end.

events.fact: The first national Thanksgiving was observed by proclamation of President George Washington, who attended worship at St. Paul's Chapel in New York and gave to imprisoned debtors.
Students at Union College in Schenectady, New York founded the Kappa Alpha Society, the first college social fraternity in America.

block: On November 26, 1789, the young nation kept its first national day of Thanksgiving by proclamation of President George Washington, who spent the day at worship in St. Paul's Chapel in New York and sent food and beer to the city's imprisoned debtors. On the same day in 1825, students at Union College in Schenectady founded the Kappa Alpha Society, the first college fraternity, binding young men together in pledged friendship and mutual duty. An Upright citizen renders thanks to God as Washington did and remembers the prisoner as he remembered the debtor, walking in gratitude and charity and keeping faithfully the bonds of brotherhood he takes upon himself.

events.fact: Macy's held its first Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York City, marching live animals from the Central Park Zoo and four bands through the streets to delight the children.
The American Statistical Association was founded in Boston, the second-oldest professional society in the nation, devoted to the honest gathering of facts about the Republic.

block: On November 27, 1924, Macy's marched its first Thanksgiving Day Parade through the streets of New York, with bands, clowns, and a menagerie of animals borrowed from the zoo, a wholesome gift of cheer to a city full of children. On the same day in 1839, a small company of men in Boston founded the American Statistical Association, devoting themselves to the patient and honest counting of facts that a free people might govern itself wisely. A Steadfast citizen holds fast to both gladness and diligence, keeping the season's joy as Macy's did and laboring faithfully at the unglamorous work of truth, trusting that the God of order blesses both the festival and the ledger kept aright.

events.fact: The Chicago Times-Herald race, the first automobile race in the United States, was won by Frank Duryea, who drove fifty-four miles through a snowstorm in just over ten hours.
The Grand Ole Opry began broadcasting from Nashville as the WSM Barn Dance, opening with the seventy-seven-year-old fiddler Uncle Jimmy Thompson.

block: On November 28, 1895, Frank Duryea won America's first automobile race, the Chicago Times-Herald contest, grinding fifty-four miles through a blinding snowstorm in just over ten hours when most rivals could not even reach the line. On the same day in 1925, the program that became the Grand Ole Opry first took to the air from Nashville, opening with a seventy-seven-year-old fiddler and beginning the longest-running radio show in the world. An Obedient citizen honors both the inventor who pressed through the storm by the discipline of his craft and the homespun music made by men who kept faithfully to a humble, honest art, for steady submission to one's calling is what builds the good and lasting things God allows men to make.

events.fact: Colorado militia under Colonel John Chivington attacked a peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho encampment at Sand Creek, killing many who believed themselves under the protection of the government.
The first Army-Navy football game was played on the Plain at West Point, where the more seasoned Navy team defeated the new Army eleven, 24 to 0.

block: On November 29, 1864, Colorado militia under Colonel John Chivington fell upon a peaceful Cheyenne and Arapaho camp at Sand Creek and slaughtered many who had trusted in the government's promise of safety, a dark and shameful deed that calls a Christian people to mourning and repentance. On the same day in 1890, cadets and midshipmen met for the first Army-Navy football game on the Plain at West Point, where the older Navy squad bested the young Army team and began a contest still played in honor each year. A Responsible citizen takes both to heart, grieving the betrayal of the innocent at Sand Creek as a wrong for which his nation must answer before a righteous God, and resolving to bear honorably the trust placed in his own hands, whether on the field of contest or in the keeping of his word.

events.fact: American and British negotiators signed the Preliminary Articles of Peace in Paris, in which Great Britain recognized the independence of the United States, signed by Adams, Franklin, Jay, and Laurens.
Samuel Langhorne Clemens, who would write as Mark Twain, was born in Florida, Missouri, and grew up in Hannibal on the Mississippi that filled his great American tales.

block: On November 30, 1782, after long and patient negotiation, John Adams, Benjamin Franklin, John Jay, and Henry Laurens signed the Preliminary Articles of Peace in Paris, by which Great Britain at last acknowledged the United States to be free and independent. On the same day in 1835, Samuel Langhorne Clemens was born in the little Missouri town of Florida, the boy who would grow up along the Mississippi and, as Mark Twain, give America some of her most enduring stories. A Steadfast citizen sees in both the fruit of long labor, for the independence won at the treaty table came only after years of unbroken resolve, even as Twain's craft was honed through a lifetime of toil, both the reward of those who do not abandon the work God has set before them.
